title: Design a Pilot Around a Real Bottleneck
subtitle: Turn a review bottleneck into a testable pilot with a baseline and decision rules.

sources.label: GitHub Docs · Measuring a Copilot trial

scenes.title: Locate the bottleneck
scenes.body: Read the queue from the time a PR becomes ready.
scenes.narration: I have two timestamps on this example pull request. The author marked it ready at ten on Monday. The first teammate commented on the code at two on Tuesday. The team counts business hours, so with a nine-to-five schedule that is seven hours on Monday and five on Tuesday, twelve in all. The baseline across forty requests is eighteen business hours. This measurement starts at readiness. It tells the manager where work is waiting after the author has asked for a review. Try tracing the same two points on a pull request from your team.
scenes.code:
Ticket → authoring → ready for review
Ready → first substantive review → merge
Baseline median wait: 18 business hours
scenes.result: Measure the interval the team wants to improve
scenes.focus: The queue starts when a PR is ready
scenes.action: Mark readiness and the first human review

scenes.title: Write a testable intervention
scenes.body: Describe the change you expect the intervention to produce.
scenes.narration: Suppose reviewers say small fixes are hard to pick up when the expected outcomes are buried in the ticket. The pilot gives every eligible change a focused diff, clear boundary tests, and a short summary. Copilot helps the author prepare that package. Ask for a prediction the team can check. We expect those pull requests to reach their first substantive review sooner. Write an eligibility rule and try two examples. The zero-quantity issue qualifies. A database migration with several services and design decisions keeps its usual process.
scenes.code:
Eligible: routine order-validator fixes
Add: scoped diff, boundary tests, PR summary
Keep the existing human review path
scenes.result: Hypothesis: reviewers pick up clearer PRs sooner
scenes.focus: The author prepares a narrower PR
scenes.action: Define what belongs in the pilot

scenes.title: Build comparable windows
scenes.body: Apply the same eligibility and collection rules.
scenes.narration: Set aside four weeks for the baseline and four for the pilot. Use the same service and the same definition of an eligible fix in both windows. Keep a small table of the task mix and which reviewers covered the queue each week. Suppose the pilot's third week had an extra reviewer. Flag it in the scorecard. That coverage could contribute to the result. This is a useful pilot design for a local decision. A historical comparison leaves several explanations open, so save the context and bring it to the review meeting.
scenes.code:
Baseline: 40 eligible PRs across four weeks
Pilot: 40 eligible PRs across four weeks
Record reviewer shifts and queue volume
scenes.result: Compare the same type of work in one service
scenes.focus: Two four-week groups use the same rule
scenes.action: Log task mix and staffing changes

scenes.title: Define the inputs
scenes.body: Decide which signals count before looking at outcomes.
scenes.narration: Agree on how to count before you start measuring. A substantive first review discusses the change. A bot result or an acknowledgment such as ‘looking soon’ leaves the clock running. Active review minutes measure time spent reading and evaluating the pull request. Material rework means the author has to change an important part of the proposed behavior, tests, or scope. A spelling suggestion is a different kind of feedback. Give reviewers two sample comments and have them label each one. Compare answers so the team starts with a common definition.
scenes.code:
Wait: ready → first human code review
Effort: active reviewer minutes on that PR
Rework: PR needs a material author revision
scenes.focus: Wait hours and active minutes measure different work
scenes.action: Write what counts as meaningful rework

scenes.title: Set the decision thresholds
scenes.body: Use a measurable target, guardrails, and stop conditions.
scenes.narration: The team sets the finish line before the results arrive. Median wait should drop from eighteen business hours to fourteen or less. Active review starts at twenty-four minutes, and the team allows three additional minutes. Twenty-four plus three gives us a twenty-seven minute limit. The rework ceiling is fifteen percent and the spending cap is three hundred dollars. Track post-merge defects with a fixed follow-up period. A serious data or access incident triggers a pause and the agreed response process. Put these rules where the decision owner can find them.
scenes.code:
Wait <= 14 h | Effort <= 27 min
Rework <= 15% | Incremental cost <= $300
Monitor post-merge defects and access incidents
scenes.result: Serious data or access incident triggers a pause
scenes.focus: The allowed effort increase is three minutes
scenes.action: Write the benefit and guardrail values

scenes.title: Launch with an evidence trail
scenes.body: Assign responsibility for evidence during the pilot.
scenes.narration: The engineering lead is accountable for the pilot record. The author and reviewer own their parts of each pull request. Use issue seventeen and pull request forty-two as the walkthrough. Read the change, check the times, and ask who would label a rework request. Schedule a quick weekly check to catch missing evidence while the team can still recover it. Before starting, hand the record to a teammate. Ask them to explain which tasks qualify, when the review clock starts, and what result would make the team pause. Fix anything they interpret differently.
scenes.code:
Pilot record: windows, eligibility, metrics, owner
Evidence exercise: issue #17 → PR #42
Weekly check: exceptions, staffing, data gaps
scenes.result: Start after the review roles are assigned
scenes.focus: Issue #17 links to the first example PR
scenes.action: Give the scorecard a named owner
